subject: Cloud Computing
title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
description: A 60-second lesson on DNS: The Internet's Phone Book.

hook.text: You type 'google.com' and a website appears. But computers only understand numbers, not names.

buildup.text: DNS translates domain names into IP addresses — the actual numerical location of each server.

discovery.text: This lookup happens in milliseconds, querying a hierarchy of DNS servers around the globe.

twist.text: DNS is a single point of failure. In 2016, a DNS attack took down Twitter, Reddit, and Netflix at once.

climax.text: Cloud providers run their own DNS services for speed and resilience. Route 53, Cloud DNS, Azure DNS.

punchline.text: Without DNS, you'd need to memorize numbers. Lots of them.

quiz.question: What is the role of DNS in cloud computing?
options: Translating human-readable domain names into numerical IP addresses
Encrypting data as it travels between servers
Storing backup copies of websites for disaster recovery

details.summary: DNS translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses that computers use to communicate. Every cloud request begins with a DNS lookup. Cloud DNS services like Route 53 and Cloud DNS add features like health-checked routing and geographic load balancing.
details.whyItMatters: DNS is the invisible first step of every internet interaction. A slow or unavailable DNS response means your application is unreachable regardless of server health.
takeaways: DNS converts domain names to IP addresses for every request
Cloud DNS services add health checks and geographic routing
DNS resolution typically takes 20 to 120 milliseconds

faq.question: What is a DNS lookup?
faq.answer: When you type a URL, your device asks a DNS resolver to find the corresponding IP address. The resolver checks its cache, then queries root servers, TLD servers, and authoritative name servers in sequence. The result is cached to speed up subsequent requests.

faq.question: How do cloud providers use DNS for routing?
faq.answer: Cloud DNS services can route users to the nearest healthy server using geographic or latency-based routing. Health checks automatically remove failed endpoints from DNS responses. Weighted routing enables gradual traffic shifts during deployments.
